correctness.rationale: For nonnegative neighboring secants \(a,b,c,d\), the Akima derivative is a weighted average of \(b,c\). The displayed algebra proves the sharp enough universal estimate \(0\le m\le(a+b+c+d)/2\), including the zero-weight convention. On a uniform grid the four secants telescope, giving \(0\le h m_i\le M/2\). In the Hermite representation, the data-value basis functions are a convex pair, while the two derivative basis functions have signs \(+,-\); their extrema are \(4/27\), so the interpolant lies between \(-2M/27\) and \(M+2M/27\). The explicit monotone family has endpoint derivatives \(\varepsilon\) and \(1/2-2\varepsilon\) and value \((104\varepsilon-2)/27\) at \(t=2/3\), approaching the lower endpoint; reversal-complement symmetry gives the upper endpoint. I independently checked the derivative lemma on the exact integer box \(0\le a,b,c,d\le8\) and the rational sharpness witness, including the strictly positive transformed value \(-2/75\).

value.rationale: Akima interpolation remains a standard local cubic method, and overshoot on monotone bounded data is a longstanding practical limitation. An exact, scale-free global defect with a sharp family and a strictly positive-data undershoot witness gives a useful method-level stability invariant and a quantitative benchmark for shape-preserving modifications.

final_claim: For the original Akima cubic rule on a uniform grid and any bi-infinite nondecreasing data sequence in \([0,M]\), the interpolant has the sharp global range \([-2M/27,29M/27]\); equivalently the maximum possible undershoot or overshoot is exactly \(2M/27\).
limitations: Original scalar Akima rule on an equally spaced grid, for interior segments.
No claim for modified Akima variants, nonuniform grids, multidimensional extensions or endpoint extrapolation.

The original 1970 Akima article was not obtained in verified complete full text; its primary abstract/bibliographic record and later technical descriptions were inspected, and an authorized institutional retrieval attempt returned an operational error.
